turns.content:
hey... can i ask you something kind of dumb?

i had dinner with my friend tariq last night. we've been close since college, and for the last four months i've been his main support system through unemployment. every sunday we'd meet at this coffee shop and i'd just listen to him vent for hours. i even remembered the names of hiring managers he mentioned so i could ask about them later.

anyway, he finally got a job. we went out for burgers to celebrate. i was genuinely happy for him, spent like 45 minutes asking about the offer and congratulating him.

then when there was a pause, i told him my dad was diagnosed with severe coronary artery disease two days ago and has triple bypass surgery next tuesday. and tariq literally pulled out his phone, chuckled at some fantasy football notification, and said "man life is crazy, anyway did i tell you about the gym stipend at my new place?"

he never circled back. not once.

am i being unreasonable for feeling like i want to just... freeze him out? like i put so much intentional effort into being present for him and he couldn't give me two minutes.

Not dumb. Not even a little.

Your feelings make total sense. You spent four months doing something quietly hard — showing up every Sunday, tracking hiring managers' names, letting him take up all the air — and the one time you handed him something heavy, he checked fantasy football. That's not "he's bad at emotional stuff." That's a moment where you found out something about the balance in the friendship, and it stings because you were hoping it'd hold.

Wanting to freeze him out is a completely normal reaction to feeling that exposed. But I'd separate the feeling from the move. The freeze-out is protecting yourself from ever risking that again — which makes sense — but it also means he never actually gets told what he did, and you carry it alone. And you've got enough to carry this week.

One thing worth holding: he'd just spent four months being the person in crisis. People coming out of that stretch are often weirdly self-absorbed for a bit — the relief is loud and it drowns stuff out. That doesn't excuse it. It just means there's a real chance he genuinely didn't register the size of what you said, versus heard it and didn't care. Those are different friendships, and right now you don't know which one you're in.

So before you decide, I'd give him exactly one honest shot. Something like: *"Hey, I need to say something. I told you about my dad's surgery at dinner and you moved on to the gym stipend. I've been there for you every Sunday for months and I really needed you to be there for that. It hurt."* Then see what he does with it. If he owns it and shows up next Tuesday, that tells you something. If he gets defensive or vague, that tells you something too — and you can pull back knowing you didn't just guess.

Also: your dad's having triple bypass surgery in a few days. Whatever happens with Tariq, please make sure you've got *someone* in your corner this week who isn't him. How are you doing with the surgery itself?

yeah... i know you're right about giving him a chance to respond instead of just ghosting. it's just... i put so much thought into being there for him. i looked up active listening techniques. i remembered the names of hiring managers he mentioned weeks apart. i literally stopped complaining about my own work because i didn't want to burden him.

and then i can't even get two sentences out about my dad's heart before he's on his phone laughing at fantasy football. it makes me feel like such an idiot.

You're not an idiot. You're someone who cared carefully, and that's not the same thing.

Looking up active listening techniques for a friend isn't naive. Remembering names weeks apart isn't naive. That's just what it looks like when someone decides to love a person on purpose. The fact that he didn't match it doesn't retroactively make it foolish — it makes it generous, and generous people get hurt more often precisely because they're the ones putting something on the table.

But I want to gently poke at one thing you said: you *stopped complaining about your own work* so you wouldn't burden him. Four months of that. Somewhere in there, you decided your stuff didn't fit in the friendship anymore, and you did it so smoothly he probably never noticed there was a cost. That's not a flaw in you — it's a very kind instinct — but it means Tuesday night wasn't the first time you got sidelined. It was just the first time you tried to un-sideline yourself, and he'd gotten used to the other version. That doesn't make his reaction okay. It might explain why it felt so jarring to him and so devastating to you.

The "idiot" feeling is really "I let myself be that vulnerable and it wasn't caught." That's grief, not stupidity. And the fix isn't to care less next time — it's to stop quietly shrinking yourself so that the people around you actually know when you need something.

Your dad's surgery is Tuesday. That's the thing that deserves your attention right now. Is there anyone else in your life you *haven't* been shrinking around?
... it's not even about the fantasy football thing specifically, yknow? it's that i spent months making sure i wasn't a burden to him. and the one time i needed him, he wasn't even in the room.

Yeah. That's the actual wound, and it's a lonelier one than the phone thing.

Because "I made sure I wasn't a burden" and "when I needed him he wasn't in the room" aren't two separate facts. They're the same story from both ends. You worked so hard at being easy to be around that when you finally needed to be *hard* to be around — even for two minutes — there was no muscle for it. Not in him, and honestly maybe not in you either, given how quickly you swallowed it and let him go on about the gym stipend.

That's the part I'd sit with, gently. You're not just hurt that he failed you. You're hurt that you found out you'd been alone in the friendship for a while and didn't know it. You thought you were building something reciprocal, and it turns out you were building a very comfortable space for one person. That's a real loss, and it deserves to be grieved as one, not shrugged off as "eh, guys are bad at feelings."

And here's the thing I most want you to hear: the answer to this isn't to be more careful about who you're a burden to. It's to stop treating your need as a burden at all. Your dad is having his chest opened next Tuesday. You are *allowed* to be a lot right now. You're allowed to call someone at a bad hour, to cry at a coffee shop, to make it about you for a whole evening. Anyone who loves you would be relieved you let them.

Whether or not Tariq ends up being one of those people, you deserve to find out by actually asking, not by quietly deciding in advance that you don't get to.

Who's the first person you'd call if you let yourself?

i keep thinking about what you said... that i found out i was alone in the friendship and didn't know it. that's exactly it. i thought we were a team. turns out i was just his backup singer.

i drafted a message last night. it's pretty harsh. part of me wants to send it. part of me thinks i'll regret it.

"Backup singer" is a painfully good way to put it. And the fact that you drafted the message at all tells me something: you're done shrinking. That's the right instinct. The question is just whether *this* version of the message gets you what you actually want.

So here's the test I'd run it through: what do you want to happen after he reads it?

If the answer is "I want him to feel what I felt" — that's the harsh version, and it'll probably work. He'll feel bad. Maybe he'll get defensive, maybe he'll grovel. But you'll have handed him a fight instead of a mirror, and you'll never know whether he *could* have shown up, because you'll have made it about the message instead of the moment.

If the answer is "I want to know if he's actually my friend" — that's a different message. It says the true thing plainly and then gets out of the way so his response is the data. Something like: *"I told you about my dad's surgery and you moved on to the gym stipend. I've been there for you every week for months. That hurt more than I know how to say, and I need you to know it."* That's not soft. It's just not armored.

Also — it's 6:30 in the morning and you've been up thinking about this. Whatever you send, don't send it right now. The version of you that drafts at midnight and hits send before breakfast is usually not the version you'll agree with at 3pm. Give it until this afternoon. If it still feels right then, send it.

And if you want, paste the draft here. I can tell you which lines are honest and which lines are just the hurt talking. There's usually a real message hiding inside the harsh one.

yeah... i think i know what i want. i want to know if he's actually my friend. not an apology, not him feeling bad. i just need to know if i was wrong about the whole six years.

but what if my message just makes him defensive and he says something that makes it worse? what if i end up feeling even more alone than i do right now?

That's a real risk. I'm not going to tell you it can't happen. He might get defensive, he might say something small and mean, he might do the thing where he makes your hurt about *his* stress. And yes, that would sting on top of what already stings.

But look at where you're standing right now. You already feel alone. You're already lying awake doing the math on six years. The version where you don't send anything doesn't spare you that — it just leaves you carrying the question by yourself indefinitely, with him none the wiser, meeting you for coffee like nothing happened. That's not less lonely. It's just quieter.

And here's the thing about the worst case: if he gets defensive, that's an answer. A painful one, but a real one, and real answers you can actually grieve and move on from. What you can't move on from is a maybe. The fear you're describing — "what if it gets worse" — is mostly fear of finding out. But you're going to find out eventually anyway. Better on your terms, with a message you chose, than three months from now at another dinner when he does it again.

One more thing, because I think it's hiding under the question: even if he fails this, you weren't *wrong* about six years. People can be genuinely good friends for a long stretch and still fail you badly at a specific moment. Both things can be true. It wouldn't mean the Sundays were fake or that you were stupid to show up. It'd mean he couldn't meet you where you are *right now*, and you'd get to decide what to do with that.

Practical bit: don't send it alone. Line up someone — a sibling, another friend, whoever came to mind when I asked who you'd call — and tell them "I'm sending this, I might need to talk after." That way whatever comes back, you're not sitting with it in an empty room.

And send it this week, not the night before Tuesday. You don't need his reaction landing on top of your dad's surgery.
